(Family Letter No. 5)
En Route Honolulu-Wake
March 1, 1950
Dear Femily,
We have just taken off from the airport in one of the
new Boeing double deckers with Wake Isiand our first port of call
eight hours and 2400 miles away. Debby and Hebe saw all of the
Hawaiian Islands. You know, there are five big islands and three
small ones.
Two of the latter cannot be visited, namely Niihau
which is owned by a family named Robinson, former missionaries
who are still very religious and do not want any sinners on their
island.
They raise cattle and do very well financially with their
unspoiled almost untouched by modern civilization paradise.
There
is a saying out here which rather sums up the history of the
Islends:
"When the missionaries first arrived they had religion
and the Hawaiians had land.
Now the natives have religion."
The
other island
where no one can go is Kahoolawe or the "Island of
Death" which is uninhabited because it is arid.
It was used during
the war as a target for air bombing, and lots of unexploded shells
are on it.
We flew over it on an aerial cruise.
It is literally
blowing away, as the sparse ground cover is pulled out by the roots
by mountain goats and the wind blows the red soil into dust storms
which often travel far out to sea. On the 22nd of February we made
an aerial cruise of all the islands to the east of Oahu (on which
is Honolulu).
We had a DC-4 with loudspeakers scattered through
the length of the cabin.
An old resident gave us a running account
and description of all the points of interest.
The small bay where
Captain Cook was killed, the snow-covered mountain on which there
is skiing, the leper colony on the island of Maui and other points
of interest.
We landed at Hilo which according to one story got
its name from an old gravestone which read, "Here In Lies Olsen".
All the small letters had faded out and only the deep carved cap-
itals remained.
As in the case of most of my stories it probably
isn't true, but that's unimportant! Hilo is the second city of
the Islands, the capital of the Island of Hawaii which is larger
than all the others put together.
Vie drove up to the Volcano
House on the edge of the crater of Kilauea for lunch.
Steam comes
out of hundreds of crevices all over the place, and for my part
if there had been just one rumble I would have said, "feet carry
me away".
After lunch we drove down to the orchid gardens where
Debby and Hebe were presented with orchid leis in each of which
were more than three hundred orchids. I told them that they have
had their respective lifetime orchid quota and not to expect any
more from me.
The business is entirely an airborne industry, and
we carry about 1,000 Ibs of orchids per day from Honolulu to
the
mainland.
As I
said above, our PAA special plane circled all the
islands east of Oahu on the 22nd. On Sunday, February 26th Debby,
lebe and 1 ilew west to kaual in a Hawaiian Airline DC-3, a fligh
We landed at the new airport at
Lihue where Debby and Pompey Bakewell were waiting for us.
They
both looked fine and there was no doubt about their pleasure in
greeting folks from the family.
They drove us to the Kauai Inn -
a most attractive small hotel where we chacked in and all had

-2-
breakfast. Then we got some box lunches and drove along the east
and north coast of Kauai as far as the road goes.
The scenery is
magnificent - blue ocean, white breakers on alternate rocky shore
and sand beaches. Some places the jungle covered mountains slant
abruptly into the sea while elsewhere fertile valleys and gentle
slopes are covered with rice-paddies or sugar cane.
It was a
"typical Lake George day". We stopped for lunch on a beach where
the breakers came in too strong for amateur swimmers, but at one
end a small rocky point jutted out to form a crystal clear pool
where we all went in.
We got back to the Inn about 4:00 o'clock
and at 5:00 Pompey called by to take us to their house for dinner
and see the thee little girls. The latter are just as cute as
they can be with dispositions
well geared to the healthy, open-air
life they lead. The house is a most attractive one-storey ranch type,
right on the ocean.
We had a perfectly delicious dinner with fried
chicken, ice cream and coconut cake.
After dinner Pompey showed us
the color film of his perents and Ruth and Steve taken and delivered
by the Archie Lees.
Also pictures of the kids, the house and local
shots including ones of the fish pond built by the Menehune or
legendary dwarfs who do all sorts of good and bad things on dark
nights when everyone is asleep.
Pompey says that the Hawaiians
explain almost any shortcoming of their own es attributable to
the Menehunes, especially if anything in the home or office di-
sappears.
The next day, Monday February 27th, we drove along the
south shore and up to the Waimes Canyon which is a 4,000 foot deep
canyon second only to the Grand Canyon of Colorado in scenic
grandeur. It is much like the Grand Canyon except that the latter
is done in technicolor while the Waimea is in various shades of
green. The road there leads through fields of sugar cane and woods
filled with colored trees, bushes and flowers.
The little towns
and small houses are picturesque and many typical of the real old
Hawaii. After late lunch at the Bakewells we flew back to Honolulu.
Hebe took some hula lessons as well es surfboard, with
the result that she used muscles never used before in the former
and
got more bruises than a Notre Dame quarterback in the latter.
She and Debby loved all the Hawaiian music that was put on at every
one of the many parties given for the P.A.A. Directors.
They had
the best quartets and orchestras, end it meally was wonderful.
This morning Debby and I met Henry Cooper on his 7:00
a.m. arrival from San Francisco - Debby with a couple of leis and
me with an aloha shirt.
We took him into the Royal Hawaiian for
breakfast and a look around before joining him on this flight.
Dave Ingalls had breekfast with us and then, while Debby and I
finished packing, drove Henry up to the Pali for a look et Honolulu.
Henry is crazy about Honolulu, and I suspect some day will return
for a longer stay.
Later - Henry and I have just come back from the cockpit
where the Captain told him all about the navigation, engines, in-
struments, etc.
Then we had a drink on the lower deck followed by
a steak dinner. He is now asleep, as is Debby. Hebe and I are about
to join them.
